title: Penicillin
description: Group of antibiotics derived from fungi
wiki_lead:
Penicillins (P, PCN or PEN) are a group of β-lactam antibiotics originally obtained from Penicillium moulds, principally P. chrysogenum and P. rubens. Eight species of Penicillium, in the section Chrysogena, produce penicillins. Most penicillins in clinical use are synthesised by P. chrysogenum using deep tank fermentation and then purified. A number of natural penicillins have been discovered, but only two purified compounds are in clinical use: penicillin G (intramuscular or intravenous use) and penicillin V (given by mouth). Penicillins were among the first medications to be effective against many bacterial infections caused by staphylococci and streptococci. They are still widely used today for various bacterial infections, though many types of bacteria have developed resistance following extensive use.
In the United States, 10% of the population claims penicillin allergies, but because the frequency of positive skin test results decreases by 10% with each year of avoidance, 90% of these patients can eventually tolerate penicillin. Additionally, those with penicillin allergies can usually tolerate cephalosporins (another group of β-lactam) because the immunoglobulin E (IgE) cross-reactivity is only 3%.
Penicillin was discovered in 1928 by the Scottish physician Alexander Fleming as a crude extract of P. rubens. Fleming's student Cecil George Paine was the first to successfully use penicillin to treat eye infection (neonatal conjunctivitis) in 1930. The purified compound (penicillin F) was isolated in 1940 by a research team led by Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain at the University of Oxford. Fleming first used the purified penicillin to treat streptococcal meningitis in 1942. The 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was shared by Chain, Fleming and Florey.
Several semisynthetic penicillins are effective against a broader spectrum of bacteria: these include the antistaphylococcal penicillins, aminopenicillins, and antipseudomonal penicillins.

Nomenclature
The term "penicillin" is defined as the natural product of Penicillium mould with antimicrobial activity. It was coined by Alexander Fleming on 7 March 1929 when he discovered the antibacterial property of Penicillium rubens. Fleming explained in his 1929 paper in the British Journal of Experimental Pathology that "to avoid the repetition of the rather cumbersome phrase 'Mould broth filtrate', the name 'penicillin' will be used". The name thus refers to the scientific name of the mould, as described by Fleming in his Nobel lecture in 1945:

I have been frequently asked why I invented the name "Penicillin". I simply followed perfectly orthodox lines and coined a word which explained that the substance penicillin was derived from a plant of the genus Penicillium just as many years ago the word "Digitalin" was invented for a substance derived from the plant Digitalis.
In modern usage penicillin is used more broadly to refer to any β-lactam antimicrobial that contains a thiazolidine ring fused to the β-lactam core and may or may not be a natural product. Like most natural products, penicillin is present in Penicillium moulds as a mixture of active constituents (gentamicin is another example of a natural product that is an ill-defined mixture of active components). grok_lead: Penicillin is a group of beta-lactam antibiotics originally derived from certain species of the mold Penicillium, particularly Penicillium chrysogenum and Penicillium rubens, which inhibit the growth of a wide range of bacteria. Discovered accidentally in 1928 by Scottish bacteriologist Alexander Fleming at St. Mary's Hospital in London, penicillin was identified when a contaminant mold in a bacterial culture plate prevented the growth of Staphylococcus aureus around it. Although Fleming published his findings, it was not until the early 1940s that a team led by Australian pathologist Howard Florey and German-British biochemist Ernst Chain at the University of Oxford successfully isolated, purified, and demonstrated the therapeutic potential of penicillin in animal models and early human trials. Their work, which enabled large-scale production during World War II, earned Fleming, Florey, and Chain the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of penicillin and its curative effects against infections. The mechanism of action of penicillin involves the beta-lactam ring in its structure, which mimics the D-alanyl-D-alanine substrate and covalently binds to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) in bacterial cells, thereby inhibiting the transpeptidase enzymes responsible for cross-linking peptidoglycan chains in the cell wall. This disruption weakens the bacterial cell wall, leading to osmotic lysis and death, particularly in actively dividing gram-positive bacteria such as streptococci and staphylococci, as well as some gram-negative cocci and anaerobes. Penicillin's narrow spectrum of activity initially limited its use, but semi-synthetic derivatives like ampicillin and amoxicillin, developed in the 1950s and 1960s, expanded its efficacy against a broader range of pathogens, including some gram-negative bacteria. Penicillin's introduction marked the dawn of the antibiotic era, transforming infectious disease treatment by reducing mortality from conditions like pneumonia, syphilis, and wound infections, and saving an estimated 200 million lives worldwide. Mass production efforts, spurred by wartime needs, involved collaboration between academic researchers and pharmaceutical companies, leading to the first clinical trials in 1941 and widespread availability by 1945. However, its overuse has contributed to the rise of antibiotic resistance, with mechanisms such as beta-lactamase production by bacteria posing ongoing challenges to its effectiveness. Today, penicillin remains a cornerstone of antimicrobial therapy, recommended as first-line treatment for many infections due to its safety profile, low cost, and efficacy when susceptibility is confirmed.
